content.prompt: Circle which unit(s) of measurement would be most appropriate to measure these areas.

answer.worked: A desktop is a modest surface: square metres give a convenient overall size, while square centimetres give a finer measurement. Correct answer: $\mathrm{m}^{2}$ or $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$.
A page has side lengths conveniently measured in centimetres, so square centimetres suit its area. Correct answer: $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$.
Square millimetres suit a tiny insect; square centimetres suit a larger insect. Correct answer: $\mathrm{mm}^{2}$ or $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$, depending on its size.
A phone's face has dimensions conveniently measured in centimetres. Correct answer: $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$.

answer.short: $\mathrm{ha}$; $\mathrm{km}^{2}$ also suits a very large farm.
answer.worked: Hectares conveniently measure agricultural land; square kilometres suit very large farms. Correct answer: $\mathrm{ha}$, or $\mathrm{km}^{2}$ for a very large farm.
A basketball court has dimensions measured in metres, so square metres give a convenient area. Correct answer: $\mathrm{m}^{2}$.
A city covers a large region, making square kilometres convenient. Correct answer: $\mathrm{km}^{2}$.
An ant's head is very small, so square millimetres suit its area. Correct answer: $\mathrm{mm}^{2}$.
A country covers a very large region, so square kilometres are suitable. Correct answer: $\mathrm{km}^{2}$.
Square metres suit a field whose dimensions are measured in metres; hectares also give a convenient measure of this large land area. Correct answer: $\mathrm{m}^{2}$ or $\mathrm{ha}$.

answer.worked:
There are $10$ squares along each side.
$$\begin{align*}N&=10\times10\\N&=100\end{align*}$$
So $100$ squares of $1\ \mathrm{mm}^2$ fit in $1\ \mathrm{cm}^2$.

inlines.text: How many mm in a cm?

answer.worked:
The length conversion factor is $10$, so the area conversion factor is $10^2$.
$$\begin{align*}1\ \mathrm{cm}^2&=10\times10\ \mathrm{mm}^2\\1\ \mathrm{cm}^2&=100\ \mathrm{mm}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Calculate the area of this rectangle, giving answer in $\text{cm}^{2}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*} 1\text{ cm}^{2} &= 10^{2}\text{ mm}^{2} \\ 21\text{ cm}^{2} &= 21\times10^{2}\text{ mm}^{2} \\ 21\text{ cm}^{2} &= 2100\text{ mm}^{2} \end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Redo the calculation by first converting $3\text{ cm}$ and $7\text{ cm}$ to mm, then calculate the area, giving answer in $\text{mm}^{2}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*} 3\text{ cm} &= 30\text{ mm} \\ 7\text{ cm} &= 70\text{ mm} \\ A &= 30\times70\text{ mm}^{2} \\ A &= 2100\text{ mm}^{2} \end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: When doing area calculations, does it matter if you first convert the lengths or convert the area at the end? Which do you prefer?

answer.short: Both methods give the same area when used correctly. Preference varies; Mr Ding recommends converting lengths first to reduce area-conversion mistakes.
answer.worked:
Both methods give the same area because the area conversion factor is the square of the length conversion factor.

$$\begin{align*} A &= (3\times7)\times10^{2}\text{ mm}^{2} = 2100\text{ mm}^{2} \\ A &= (3\times10)(7\times10)\text{ mm}^{2} = 2100\text{ mm}^{2} \end{align*}$$

Preference varies. For example, I prefer converting lengths first. Mr Ding recommends this approach because students tend to make mistakes converting units of area.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the height in centimetres and $b$ the base in centimetres.
$$\begin{align*}b&=3h\\A&=bh\\75&=3h\times h\\75&=3h^2\\h^2&=25\\h&=5\text{ cm}\\b&=15\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: A path 1.8 m wide is being built around a rectangular garden.
The garden is 8.4 m long and 5.4 m wide. The path is shaded in the diagram.
The path is to be covered with triangular pavers with side lengths of 15 cm and 20 cm as shown. How many pavers are needed?

spec.description: A rectangular garden inside an outer rectangle, with restrained diagonal hatching identifying the surrounding path. Preserve all four dimension arrows, the Garden label and NOT TO SCALE.
spec.mathematics: The inner rectangle measures 8.4 m by 5.4 m. The path is 1.8 m wide on every side. Dimension arrows above and right of the inner rectangle measure the garden; arrows across the left and bottom strips measure path width.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and region labels are visible; outer dimensions and calculated areas are absent.

spec.description: One right triangular paver, with a vertical left side, horizontal bottom side and hypotenuse descending to the right. Preserve the right-angle marker, One paver heading and NOT TO SCALE.
spec.mathematics: The perpendicular sides are 15 cm and 20 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied lengths and right-angle marker are visible.

answer.worked:
The path adds $1.8\ \text{m}$ on each side of the garden.
$$\begin{align*}
L_{\text{outer}} &= 8.4+2\times1.8=12\ \text{m} \\
W_{\text{outer}} &= 5.4+2\times1.8=9\ \text{m} \\
A_{\text{path}} &= 12\times9-8.4\times5.4 \\
A_{\text{path}} &= 62.64\ \text{m}^{2} \\
A_{\text{path}} &= 626400\ \text{cm}^{2} \\
A_{\text{paver}} &= \frac12\times20\times15 \\
A_{\text{paver}} &= 150\ \text{cm}^{2} \\
N_{\text{pavers}} &= \frac{626400}{150} \\
N_{\text{pavers}} &= 4176
\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $4176$ pavers are needed.

Thus the upper pennant height is 0.7+0.6, the lower pennant height is 0.6+1.4, and the shared triangle has perpendicular sides 0.6 and 2-1.4=0.6. answer.worked:

$$\begin{align*}
A_1&=\frac12(0.6+0.7)\times2\\

answer.worked:
Let $A_p$ be the parallelogram's area and $A_r$ the rectangle's area.
$$\begin{align*}
A_p &= bh\\
A_p &= 12\times7\\
A_p &= 84\text{ cm}^2
\end{align*}$$
The rectangle has half this area.
$$\begin{align*}
A_r &= 84\div2\\
A_r &= 42\text{ cm}^2\\
A_r &= lw\\
42 &= 8x\\
\frac{42}{8} &= x\\
5.25\text{ cm} &= x
\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Three unfilled adjoining squares increase in size from left to right, share a horizontal bottom baseline and form a stepped exterior.
spec.mathematics: The square areas are 36 cm², 64 cm² and 81 cm². The coordinate side lengths are derived from those areas without printing the resulting lengths. Shared vertical boundaries are dashed; exterior step edges are solid.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the three supplied area labels are visible.

answer.short: $64\text{ cm}$. Square sides are $6,8,9\text{ cm}$; add the exterior edges.
answer.worked:
Using $A=l^2$, find each square's side length.
$$\begin{align*}l_1^2&=36\\l_1&=6\text{ cm}\\l_2^2&=64\\l_2&=8\text{ cm}\\l_3^2&=81\\l_3&=9\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
The bottom edge is $6+8+9=23\text{ cm}$; the exposed steps are $9-8=1\text{ cm}$ and $8-6=2\text{ cm}$. Add the exterior edges clockwise from the bottom.
$$\begin{align*}P&=23+9+9+1+8+2+6+6\\P&=64\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
